# The Day the River Turns

Once a year, on the first Tuesday after the thaw, the Aldern River runs backward.

Nobody in Merrow's Crossing remembers when it started. My grandmother said it had always done it, and her grandmother said the same, so either it truly has, or the women in my family are liars going back a long way. I've never been able to decide which I'd prefer.

It happens around dawn. The water slows, the way a person slows when they think they've heard their name called from another room. For a few minutes it barely moves at all. The ducks get confused. Then, with a sound like a long breath drawn in, the whole brown body of it turns and starts climbing back toward the hills.

That's when we put the letters in.

---

The rule is simple. You write to someone upstream, and upstream doesn't mean a place. The river going backward carries things backward, and not only in distance. You fold your letter into a boat or seal it in a jar or just let it go loose, and the current takes it to the past.

Nobody can prove this. That's the first thing people from outside say when they hear about it, usually with a little smile, as if they're the first to think of it. They're right. Nobody can prove it. But I've noticed that the people who smile hardest are the ones who stand longest on the bank afterward, watching.

---

My father ran the ferry until his hands got too bad for the ropes. After that he sat on the porch and watched other people run it badly. He never wrote a letter on River Day. Not once. My mother wrote every year, long ones, pages folded into fat little parcels she wrapped in wax paper. She never told us who they were for.

When I was eleven, I asked my father why he didn't write.

He was quiet for so long I thought he hadn't heard. Then he said, "Because I'm afraid it works."

I didn't understand. I thought that was the whole point, that you *wanted* it to work. He tried to explain. If you could send a letter back, you might change something. And if you changed something, then maybe the life you were standing in right now, with its porch and its bad hands and its daughter asking foolish questions, might just quietly stop being true.

"I made a lot of mistakes," he said. "But you came out of all of them. I'm not risking you for a do-over."

I didn't say anything. I was eleven. But I've thought about it every River Day since.

---

My mother died in the autumn I turned thirty. We found her letters afterward, or some of them, drafts she hadn't sent, or copies she kept. I'm still not sure which. They were addressed to a girl named Tess.

It took me a long time to understand that Tess was her. My mother at nineteen, at twenty-two, at twenty-six. Every year she had written to a younger version of herself, and every year she'd said almost the same thing.

She didn't say *don't marry him*, or *leave this town*, or *take the job in the city*. She didn't warn herself about anything. Mostly she told Tess what was coming, the good parts. *You'll have a daughter who sings to the cat when she thinks no one's listening. You'll learn to make bread and be terrible at it for years and then suddenly good. There's a winter where the river freezes solid and the whole town skates on it by lantern light, and you'll fall, and he'll laugh, and you'll be furious, and it will be one of the best nights of your life.*

At the bottom of every letter, the same line:

*Don't be so scared. It turns out all right. Not perfect. All right.*

---

I think about my parents often, the two ways they stood on that bank. My father kept his hands in his pockets because he loved the present too much to touch the past. My mother reached back every year to hold her own hand.

I used to think one of them was wrong. Now I think they were each protecting the same thing from opposite sides.

---

This morning I got up before dawn and walked down to the water. There was mist on the fields, and the usual crowd had gathered along the bank: old Mr. Fenwick with his shoebox, the Adeyemi twins with paper boats, a young man I didn't recognize holding a single envelope like it might bite him.

I had a letter too. I'd written it at the kitchen table the night before, and rewritten it, and rewritten it again, until the pages were soft from handling.

I didn't ask for anything to change. I don't have my father's courage to leave things alone, or my mother's gift for knowing exactly what to say. But I had something in between.

The river slowed. The ducks complained. Then came that long indrawn breath, and the water turned for home.

I knelt and set my letter on the surface and watched it spin once before the current caught it.

It was addressed to a man on a porch with bad hands, on an evening about twenty years ago, when a little girl asked him a question he didn't know how to answer.

It said only:

*She understood. Eventually. She's all right.*
